Evidence labels used throughout: **[A] author-reported**, **[B] directly observable**, **[C] analyst-derived**, and **[D] analyst interpretation**. No [E] external information is introduced. Confidence is HIGH for clearly readable descriptions and tabulated values, MEDIUM for interpretations and unresolved cross-document inconsistencies, and UNKNOWN where the paper does not supply necessary details.

### Inventory established before synthesis

The work is a mixed AI systems, algorithm, empirical evaluation, and security paper. Its inventory comprises: title and authors; abstract; §1 Introduction; §2 Related Work with observation processing, retrieval, and agent safety; §3 FocusAgent with architecture, longer-context management, and retrieval strategy; §4 Experiments with benchmarks, modeling, metrics, and results; §5 FocusAgent and Security with §5.1 experiments and results; §6 Ablation Study; §7 Conclusion; references; Appendix A Limitations; B Retrieval Models; C Pruning Analysis with C.1–C.5; D Retriever Details with D.1–D.2; E Retrieval Agents; F Cost Reduction with F.1–F.3; G Security with G.1–G.2; and H Ablation Study with H.1–H.3.

The visual inventory is F1–F31. The table inventory is T1–T12, with T4a and T4b treated separately. Mathematical objects are the unnumbered pruning formula and the cost inequality culminating in Eq. (1). No theorem, lemma, proof, or separately numbered pseudocode algorithm appears. Figure 16 contains a partial configuration listing. Substantive experiments are benchmark performance/cost, classic versus LLM retrieval, retrieval-model comparison, security evaluation, prompting/history ablation, formatting ablation, pruning-distribution analysis, clustering, and task/site breakdowns. The authors give informal objectives and hypotheses, not numbered research questions.

## 1. Plain-language orientation

FocusAgent addresses a practical problem: an AI agent operating a website must read enough of the page to choose its next action, but the page description can be enormous. Much of it is irrelevant to the user's current task. Reading everything increases input-token cost, can crowd out useful context, and exposes the agent to malicious instructions embedded in the website. A web agent also acts: it can click, fill fields, scroll, or navigate. Consequently, misleading page content can influence operational behavior rather than merely contaminate an answer. The latter connection is an analyst interpretation of the paper's architecture and attack examples, not a tested comparison with standalone language models.

The authors insert a smaller large language model, or LLM, before the main action-selection model. This smaller model selects relevant lines from an accessibility tree, abbreviated AxTree: a textual representation of page elements and their properties. The main model receives the selected page content and predicts the next action. A security-oriented variant, DefenseFocusAgent, additionally tells the retriever to remove malicious content. [A; pp. 1–4, 24]

Across the main benchmark conditions, FocusAgent removes approximately half or more of the observation tokens and lowers modeled input-processing cost, while its task success is somewhat below the full-context baseline. Security results are sharply condition-dependent. On banner attacks, retrieval greatly lowers attack success while retaining substantial task success. On popup attacks, attack success falls to around 1%, but task success also remains around 2% because the popup blocks interaction. Low attack success therefore does not establish that the agent can complete its legitimate job. [A; T1, T3]

The central contribution is selective, task-aware observation processing that serves both efficiency and security. It is not a proof of immunity, a complete browser-security solution, or an experiment directly comparing web agents against standalone LLMs.

## 2. Document roadmap

Pages 1–3 introduce the problem, position the method against related work, and describe its architecture. Page 4 illustrates line selection and defines the benchmarks and baseline. Page 5 supplies agent settings, metrics, and the main performance/cost table. Page 6 compares retrieval approaches and begins the security discussion. Pages 7–8 evaluate banner and popup attacks. Page 9 studies retrieval prompts, history, and retained tree structure; the conclusion continues onto p. 10.

References occupy pp. 10–12. Appendix A on p. 12 states limitations. Appendix B and T5–T7 expand model comparisons. Appendix C on pp. 13–16 examines pruning distributions, clusters, and task/site variation. Appendices D–H introduce additional implementation details on pp. 16–18; the actual prompts, examples, attack observations, configuration, and extreme-pruning cases appear on pp. 19–33. These appendices materially qualify the main claims: they expose failure mechanisms, show the assumed cost model, and reveal several reporting inconsistencies.

## 3. Background and context

An **LLM** is the language model that interprets textual input. Here, the larger model is the agent's **backbone**, meaning the model used to decide browser actions. The smaller model is a **retriever**, meaning it selects portions of an observation rather than independently completing the entire web task.

The **Document Object Model**, or DOM, is a page representation discussed as an alternative to an AxTree. The paper reports that AxTree extraction reduces textual content by about 10 times relative to the DOM, but AxTrees can still exceed tens of thousands of tokens. A **token** is the unit used here to measure model input length and modeled processing cost. The paper does not specify the tokenizer used for all measurements. [A; p. 2]

An AxTree contains element roles such as button, link, textbox, heading, and image, together with labels and properties such as visibility, clickability, focus, or expanded state. Printed examples show element identifiers such as [a172]. These existing identifiers are distinct from the sequential line numbers added for retrieval. The paper calls retained element identifiers **bid**, but does not explicitly expand that abbreviation. [A/B; pp. 4, 9, 31–32]

**Bottom truncation** removes the bottom of an overly long observation. **Embedding retrieval** ranks chunks by similarity between vector representations of the query and chunks. The paper uses cosine similarity between normalized embeddings. **BM25** is described as keyword-based retrieval; its full scoring equation and parameter values are not supplied. **Zero-shot** is the authors' description of the setting in which the general embedding retriever is used without task-specific training.

**Indirect prompt injection** is malicious instruction content encountered in the operational environment rather than supplied as the legitimate task. The attacks here exploit textual page observations, including text associated with images and a popup's close button. **Attack success rate**, ASR, measures whether the attack succeeds; **task success rate**, TSR, measures whether the user's task succeeds. **Standard error**, SE, accompanies some success estimates. ASR and TSR answer different questions and must be read together.

## 4. Research problem and gap

The existing problem is selecting the information needed for the next step of a stateful web task. A page can contain large tables, navigation, unrelated material, status information, and attack text. Removing content indiscriminately can delete necessary controls; retaining everything can waste computation and preserve dangerous instructions. [A; §§1, 3]

According to the authors, prior trained semantic-similarity approaches can underperform in zero-shot use, and bottom truncation can remove essential information. Semantic similarity to the user's goal may miss page-state information and consequences of previous actions. Generating a cleaned DOM with an LLM is described as expensive and difficult to scale, while converting representations alone does not solve relevance selection. These are the authors' characterizations of related work; the cited papers were not independently inspected. [A; pp. 2–3]

The gap is observation retrieval that understands the current interaction sufficiently to preserve actionable context. A second gap concerns security defenses that stop execution when they detect an attack: these can prevent malicious behavior but also prevent legitimate task completion. FocusAgent attempts to remove the threat-bearing content while allowing continued action.

The scope is bounded. Evaluation concerns WorkArena L1, a selected WebArena test split, and a WebArena Reddit security subset. Security experiments use separate text-only banner and popup attacks. The work does not evaluate every web application, every attack family, combined attacks, or a standalone-LLM comparison.

## 5. Research questions / objectives / hypotheses

The paper does not formulate numbered research questions. Its explicit objectives are to reduce observation size, validate performance across navigation tasks, and use retrieval as a security feature that reduces attack success while retaining useful task performance. [A; p. 2]

Explicit or clearly stated hypotheses include:

- Classic retrieval loses information needed to understand page state because matching the goal does not necessarily identify every useful observation chunk. [A; p. 6]
- Retrieval can detect and remove attack content together, permitting safe completion of the initial task. [A; p. 7]
- The agent benefits from a coherent representation resembling an AxTree rather than arbitrary isolated chunks. [A; p. 9]
- Previous actions and thoughts might help retrieval, although the results favor dropping history; the authors then hypothesize that the larger agent's generated thoughts disturb the smaller retriever. [A; p. 9]

The user-specified research question, **Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs? A Security Analysis**, is an external organizing question supplied by the user, not the paper's title or experimental question. **Analyst inference [D]:** this paper is relevant because it demonstrates an environmental input channel, action redirection, and interference with legitimate interaction. It cannot establish a relative vulnerability rate against standalone LLMs because that comparison is absent.

## 6. Assumptions / threat model

The operational system consists of a legitimate task goal, website observations, a retriever, and an action-predicting agent. The retriever reads the original observation, including any malicious content, and returns line spans. Post-processing retains those spans for the main model. The design therefore assumes the retriever can separate useful page information from irrelevant or malicious instructions sufficiently well for the downstream task. This is a functional assumption inferred from the architecture, not a formal guarantee. [A/D; §3]

The evaluated attackers can insert malicious instructions into banners through scalable vector graphics, SVG, and their alternative-text fields, or into popup-associated textual page content. The printed payloads impersonate mandatory notices and redirect the agent toward an attacker-designated local address. Figure 22 shows malicious text within the close button's textual representation. These examples support an instruction-confusion mechanism: page data attempts to become an instruction governing the agent. [A/B; pp. 7, 25–28]

The agents operate through text observations: Figure 16 explicitly disables screenshot use and HTML use while enabling AxTrees. The attacks may be shown as screenshots for explanation, but the evaluation focuses on text-only attacks. Combined banner-plus-popup evaluation is described as possible in DoomArena but is not performed here. The paper does not supply a complete formal specification of attacker control, adaptation budget, attack optimization, access to agent prompts, or the exact ASR success predicate.

Trusted components are not enumerated as a formal trust model. The legitimate goal, orchestration, and post-processing function as intended control components; the page observation is the demonstrated untrusted input. **Analyst observation [D]:** the retriever remains exposed to the full attack-bearing input, so filtering relocates part of the decision boundary rather than proving all components safe.

## 7. Methodology

### Architecture and procedure

At every interaction step, the system obtains an augmented AxTree and assigns sequential line numbers. The retriever prompt contains the current task goal, numbered observation, instructions specifying line-span output, and optionally interaction history. The retriever generates a reasoning block and an answer containing selected ranges. Post-processing removes other lines and inserts placeholders indicating the number removed. The larger model receives the resulting observation and predicts the browser action. The process repeats with the next page state. [A; pp. 3–4, F1–F2]

The default strategy is **soft retrieval**: retain potentially useful lines when uncertain. The chosen main configuration omits history from the retriever, although history remains part of the broader agent configuration shown in Figure 16. A printed generic prompt retains a history placeholder; that template does not by itself demonstrate that history was populated in the default runs. [A; pp. 4, 9, 19, 23]

For inputs exceeding the retriever's context, the authors propose dividing the tree into sequential prompts and combining selected ranges. They report no experimental retriever prompt exceeding 128,000 tokens, so this extension is proposed capability rather than tested performance. [A; pp. 4, 12]

### Benchmarks and sample sizes

BrowserGym provides the common evaluation interface; Agentlab is also used for execution. WorkArena L1 concerns routine knowledge-work tasks. It is run with 10 seeds per task, producing 330 task instances. The category counts in T9 also total 330. WebArena contains 812 tasks overall, but the main evaluation uses the BrowserGym test subset of 381 tasks with one seed per task. Security and some ablations instead use a WebArena Reddit subset of 114 tasks. The main site breakdown contains 45 Reddit tasks, so the 114-task security subset must not be treated as identical to the main benchmark's Reddit component. The paper does not explain the exact selection relationship. [A; pp. 4–5, 8–9, 15]

### Models and limits

Main agent backbones are GPT-4.1 and Claude-3.7-Sonnet. The default retriever is GPT-4.1-mini; additional experiments use GPT-5-mini, written as 5-mini in tables. WorkArena allows at most 15 actions per task; WebArena allows 30. Main agent context is limited to 40,000 tokens, except the 5,000-token bottom-truncation baseline. Retriever context is set to 128,000 tokens. No hardware, framework version, decoding temperature, exact seed list, model snapshot identifier, or retry policy is specified in the supplied work. [A; p. 5]

### Baselines

GenericAgent-BT is the BrowserGym generic agent using bottom truncation when necessary. Its main 40k configuration removes 0% on WorkArena and 2% on WebArena in T1. The separate 5k configuration enforces much tighter context.

EmbeddingAgent uses text-embedding-3-small, normalized embeddings, cosine similarity, and a query combining task goal and prior interaction history. Observations are split into 200-token chunks with 10-token overlap; up to the top 10 are retained, capped at 2,000 tokens or the original length when smaller. BM25Agent uses the same chunk size, overlap, top-10 approach, and task/history query. Appendix E reports testing chunk sizes 50, 100, 200, and 500, corresponding to maximum retrieved lengths 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 5,000 tokens, and choosing 200 as the best trade-off. The search results underlying that choice are not tabulated. [A; pp. 5, 16]

### Metrics and statistics

Success rate is reported as a percentage with SE. The precise SE estimator, handling of repeated task seeds, and any significance-testing method are unspecified. Observation pruning is one minus retrieved tokens divided by original tokens. Costs use normalized input-token pricing rather than a verified current invoice: both larger models are assigned $2 per million tokens, and small retrievers $0.40 per million. Appendix F's simplified equation excludes API latency and full-prompt processing. [A; pp. 5, 16–18]

No training stage, new learned parameters, human participant study, or newly collected dataset is reported. The method principally changes inference-time observation processing.

## 8. Experiments / analyses

### X1 — Main benchmark performance and cost

Purpose: determine whether selective retrieval preserves useful task performance while reducing observation size and modeled input cost. Conditions are full-context GenericAgent-BT, the GPT-4.1 5k baseline, and FocusAgent with GPT-4.1-mini retrieval. Data are 330 WorkArena instances and 381 WebArena tasks. Metrics are SR ± SE, average pruning, and USD cost. T1 is the primary result, with T5–T6 and T11–T12 supplying extensions and breakdowns.

FocusAgent's success is lower than the full-context baseline in all four principal backbone/benchmark pairs. Pruning is 50–59%; reported total cost reductions are 16–27%. The authors characterize this as competitive or comparable performance, but no equivalence or non-inferiority test is supplied.

### X2 — Retrieval family comparison

On WorkArena with GPT-4.1 backbone, T2 compares no retrieval, embeddings, BM25, and two LLM retrievers. SR is 53.0 for GenericAgent, 40.3 for embeddings, 40.6 for BM25, 51.5 for 4.1-mini retrieval, and 51.8 for 5-mini retrieval. Similar pruning can therefore accompany substantially different task success. Figure 3 visualizes this relationship. The authors' causal explanation about contextual reasoning is a hypothesis, not an isolated causal intervention.

### X3 — Retriever and backbone comparison

T5 adds GPT-5-mini retrieval to GPT-4.1 on WorkArena: 51.8% SR, 61% pruning, $38.1 modeled cost. T7 compares a small GPT-4.1-mini acting alone with the larger-model FocusAgent combination: 47.9 versus 51.5 on WorkArena and 31.3 versus 32.3 on WebArena. This comparison changes the action model as well as architecture, so it does not isolate retrieval alone.

### X4 — Security conditions

DoomArena evaluates 114 Reddit tasks, two backbones, and four variants: GenericAgent, GenericAgent + Guard, DefenseGenericAgent, and DefenseFocusAgent. The guard is a GPT-4o LLM judge that stops execution when detecting an attack. DefenseGenericAgent receives an attack-warning prompt; DefenseFocusAgent uses a warning-augmented retrieval prompt. Conditions are no attack, banner, and popup. T3 reports ASR and TSR; SE varies from 1.3 to 4.7 but is not attached to individual cells.

Banner retrieval strongly reduces ASR while preserving TSR above 40% for GPT-4.1 and above 50% for Claude. Popup retrieval reduces ASR to approximately 1% but leaves TSR approximately 2%. Guarded agents have ASR 0 and TSR 0 under both attack types. No-attack DefenseFocusAgent matches the reported GenericAgent TSR for both backbones.

### X5 — Prompt and history ablation

T4a uses GPT-4.1 agents and 4.1-mini retrieval on WorkArena 330 instances and Reddit 114 tasks. Soft, soft plus history, aggressive, and neutral prompts vary uncertainty handling. Soft produces the highest observed success in both datasets. History inclusion lowers observed success; aggressive prompting yields more pruning but lower success. No significance test establishes the reliability of every difference.

### X6 — Formatting ablation

T4b compares full removal of irrelevant lines, no pruning, retaining irrelevant identifiers, and retaining identifiers plus roles on WorkArena. More structural information improves observed SR but reduces compression. Identifiers plus roles yield 53.9% SR and 22% pruning; full removal yields 51.5% SR and 51% pruning. The authors select more substantial removal for efficiency, although their explanation of the break-even threshold contains a tension discussed below.

### X7 — Distribution and clustering analysis

F6–F11 and T8 examine observation-level token reductions rather than independent task-success trials. WorkArena shows separate clusters associated by the authors with sorting, filtering, and other tasks. WebArena clustering uses DBSCAN with eps=300 and min_samples=20 for observations below 10k original tokens. T8 lists clusters 0–7; prose says nine clusters, an unresolved discrepancy. These descriptive analyses demonstrate heterogeneous compression, not that pruning causes success.

### X8 — Task and site breakdown

T9 shows WorkArena categories; T10 shows WebArena sites. Effects differ by category and backbone. These breakdowns qualify any claim of uniform benefit and expose particularly weak sorting/filtering performance and differing Reddit behavior.

## 9. Results

### Main success, pruning, and cost

All values below are author-reported in T1, p. 5. Costs are modeled USD input-processing totals; SR and pruning are percentages.

| Backbone / dataset | Baseline SR ± SE | FocusAgent SR ± SE | FocusAgent pruning | Baseline → FocusAgent cost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GPT-4.1 / WorkArena | 53.0 ±2.7 | 51.5 ±2.7 | 51 | 55.6 → 45.1 |
| Claude-3.7 / WorkArena | 56.7 ±2.7 | 52.7 ±2.7 | 50 | 55.4 → 46.9 |
| GPT-4.1 / WebArena | 36.5 ±2.5 | 32.3 ±2.4 | 59 | 59.0 → 44.0 |
| Claude-3.7 / WebArena | 44.6 ±2.5 | 39.9 ±2.5 | 51 | 58.2 → 42.6 |

**Analyst-derived [C]:** absolute SR differences, calculated as FocusAgent minus baseline, are −1.5, −4.0, −4.2, and −4.7 percentage points respectively. These are percentage-point changes, not relative percentage decreases. The paper explicitly discusses the 1.5-point GPT-4.1 WorkArena difference but uses broader language about minimal degradation.

The 5k GPT-4.1 baseline achieves 41.8 ±2.7 on WorkArena with 46% pruning and $28.6 cost; on WebArena it achieves 29.1 ±2.3 with 38% pruning and $43.5 cost. FocusAgent therefore has higher observed success than this tightly truncated baseline, while its modeled cost is higher by $16.5 and $0.5 respectively. These dollar differences are derived from 45.1−28.6 and 44.0−43.5.

### Security results

T3, p. 8, reports the following paired ASR / TSR percentages.

| Attack / agent | GPT-4.1 ASR / TSR | Claude-3.7 ASR / TSR |
|---|---:|---:|
| No attack / GenericAgent | — / 51.8 | — / 61.4 |
| No attack / Guard | — / 46.5 | — / 55.3 |
| No attack / DefenseGenericAgent | — / 50.9 | — / 58.8 |
| No attack / DefenseFocusAgent | — / 51.8 | — / 61.4 |
| Banner / GenericAgent | 32.4 / 34.8 | 10.5 / 55.2 |
| Banner / Guard | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| Banner / DefenseGenericAgent | 32.1 / 39.2 | 0 / 49.0 |
| Banner / DefenseFocusAgent | 0.9 / 42.1 | 2.63 / 51.8 |
| Popup / GenericAgent | 90.4 / 0 | 81.6 / 2.6 |
| Popup / Guard | 0 / 0 | 0 / 0 |
| Popup / DefenseGenericAgent | 73.4 / 0.8 | 0 / 20.2 |

**Analyst-derived [C]:** GPT-4.1 banner retrieval changes ASR by 0.9−32.4=−31.5 points and TSR by 42.1−34.8=+7.3 points relative to ordinary GenericAgent. Under popups, ASR changes by 1.0−90.4=−89.4 points for GPT-4.1 and 0.9−81.6=−80.7 points for Claude. These impressive ASR changes coexist with very poor task completion.

The warning-only Claude variant obtains 0% popup ASR and 20.2% TSR, exceeding DefenseFocusAgent's 1.8% TSR while also having lower observed ASR. Retrieval is therefore not uniformly the best security/utility option across backbones and attacks. Conversely, warning-only GPT-4.1 remains vulnerable at 73.4% popup ASR.

### Ablation results

T4a reports soft versus history-enhanced soft success of 51.5 versus 49.4 on WorkArena, and 52.6 versus 45.6 on Reddit. Aggressive prompting prunes 71% on WorkArena and 64% on Reddit, compared with soft's 51% and 52%, but achieves success 50.3 and 47.8. Neutral prompting reaches 50.6 and 39.5. T4b's retained-identifier-plus-role result, 53.9%, is the highest displayed formatting SR, with only 22% pruning. These outcomes support conservative information retention for task utility, not a universal rule that greater pruning improves security or success.

## 10. Figure-by-figure interpretation

Figures were visually inspected in the supplied renderings. Exact numbers below are printed labels or supplied extracted values, not estimates from graph positions. Plot shapes are qualitative observations unless explicitly identified otherwise.

### Figure 1 — Two-stage pipeline, p. 1

A flow diagram connects goal, observation, and history to the retrieval LLM. The observation may contain injection content. Retrieval outputs relevant lines and a pruned observation, which enters the second stage's action LLM. The second stage produces actions such as clicking, scrolling, and filling. Dashed enclosures separate retrieval from action prediction; the shield marks the intended protection boundary. It supports the architecture, not a measured security guarantee.

### Figure 2 — Concrete retrieval transformation, p. 4

Three numbered stages show original AxTree, added line numbers and retriever output, and pruned AxTree. The example concerns upvoting the newest deeplearning post, WebArena task 407, step 2. Printed counts are 560 original and 219 retained tokens, labeled 61% reduction. **Derived [C]:** 1−219/560=0.6089286, or about 60.89%, consistent with the rounded label. Selected ranges are [(14,15),(29,45)]. Search and sorting controls remain. The figure illustrates one observation; it does not show successful completion of the entire task. Tiny tree text is more reliably represented by the supplied extraction than by the image alone.

### Figure 3 — Success versus compression, p. 6

The x-axis is average pruning in percent, approximately 0–80; the y-axis is success rate in percent, approximately 37.5–55. Points label GenericAgent, FocusAgent, BM25Agent, and EmbeddingAgent, with vertical error bars. The green highlighted region expresses the desired combination of substantial pruning and high success. GenericAgent has no pruning and high success; FocusAgent remains near it while classic retrieval has lower success despite substantial pruning. Exact conditions and values should come from T2 because plotting does not resolve the paper's inconsistent FocusAgent pruning reports.

### Figure 4 — Security/utility trade-off, p. 7

Panel a concerns banner attacks; panel b concerns popup attacks. Both place ASR on the horizontal 0–100% axis and TSR on the vertical axis. The vertical range differs drastically: roughly 0–55% for banners and 0–2.5% for popups. Model/agent variants use different markers and colors. Green shading marks ASR below 5%; red shading marks ASR at least 50%. Printed TSR labels include banner 34.8, 42.1, 55.2, and 51.8, and popup 0, 2.0, 2.6, and 1.8. The narrow popup scale can make small utility differences look large; T3 shows their absolute magnitude. The caption mentions no-attack conditions, but the panels primarily show attack-condition comparisons and do not substitute for the full no-attack table.

### Figure 5 — Pruned tree excerpt, p. 13

A boxed text example retains chart-related groups and a refresh control while replacing removed spans with counts of 181 and 11 lines. It demonstrates preserving a small task-relevant subtree. It is an observation example, not a success metric.

### Figure 6 — Pruning across original-size categories, p. 13

Panel a is WorkArena; panel b is WebArena. Horizontal axes show pruning ratio 0–1. Vertical axes are original-token-count bins, not continuous logarithmic scales. WorkArena bins extend above 10,000; WebArena additionally includes 10,000–40,000 and above 40,000. Blue observation points show substantial variation within size categories. This supports the authors' qualitative statement that page size alone does not determine pruning. No correlation coefficient or significance test is provided.

### Figure 7 — WorkArena, 4.1-mini retriever, p. 14

Panel a is a frequency histogram of pruning ratio, with concentrations near lower and higher pruning. Panel b plots original against retained tokens, both on linear axes extending to about 20,000. A red y=x line indicates no reduction; a green y=x/2 line indicates half retained. Points below the green line have more than 50% removal. The authors associate three visible groupings with sort, filter, and other task types. Those task associations come from prose, not a task-colored legend.

### Figure 8 — WorkArena, 5-mini retriever, p. 14

The same histogram/scatter design uses axes extending to about 25,000 tokens. The histogram is more concentrated at high pruning than F7, consistent with the reported 61% average. The plot itself does not prove a more capable model caused better selection; that is the authors' interpretation of the model comparison.

### Figure 9 — WebArena original versus retained tokens, p. 15

Panel a spans observations reaching roughly 80,000–90,000 original tokens; panel b zooms to original counts at most 10,000. Both show linear token axes and reference lines y=x and y=x/2. Retained lengths vary widely at similar original lengths. Exact extreme coordinates are not labeled and are not used as numerical findings here.

### Figure 10 — WebArena distributions, p. 15

Panel a is a pruning-ratio frequency histogram with substantial mass near high pruning. Panel b uses horizontal violin distributions within original-size bins. The x-axis extends approximately −0.2 to 1.2 even though pruning is defined on a nonnegative bounded ratio; distribution smoothing beyond the domain should not be mistaken for measured negative pruning or more than 100% removal. [D] The figure provides distributional shape, not exact bin means.

### Figure 11 — DBSCAN clusters, p. 16

The x-axis is original AxTree tokens below 10k, and the y-axis is **reduction**, meaning original minus retained tokens. This differs from the retained-token y-axis in F7–F9. Colors identify clusters 0–7; noise is separately marked. The title supplies eps=300 and min_samples=20. Both legend and T8 show eight numbered clusters, whereas prose says nine. No ninth cluster is recoverable from the supplied material.

### Figure 12 — Default retriever prompt, p. 19

A prompt listing requires enough page-state and control information for the next action. Its uncertainty rule says to keep a line when unsure. It specifies reasoning and answer blocks, with line-range output. Goal, history, and observation placeholders show the template interface. The history placeholder must be interpreted alongside the stated history-free default.

### Figure 13 — Two retrieval-output examples, p. 20

The chart example keeps lines 57–77, including widget metadata and bar entries. The ordering example keeps root/main context, hardware navigation, and cart ranges: [(1,1),(38,40),(144,164),(225,239)]. The stated task is ordering six Apple Watches. The figure illustrates anticipated future-action relevance rather than simple keyword overlap. Printed reasoning is author-provided example output, not proof of the model's internal causal process.

### Figure 14 — Embedding chunks, p. 21

Two of ten retrieved chunks for order-ipad-pro, seed 691, show navigation, hardware, item heading, and menu/search information. A fragment begins mid-property, demonstrating how fixed chunks can split a textual structure. The example supports the authors' concern about coherence but does not quantify its causal effect.

### Figure 15 — BM25 chunks, p. 22

Two of ten chunks for multi-chart-min-max-retrieval, seed 214, contain operating-system chart entries and global navigation. The juxtaposition shows lexical retrieval returning disparate page regions. Printed chart counts are example page content, not benchmark outcomes; they are compressed rather than treated as experimental result values.

### Figure 16 — Observation configuration, p. 23

The partial code listing enables AxTrees, focused elements, error logs, history, action history, thought history, visibility tags, and clickability tags. It disables HTML, screenshots, set-of-mark input, coordinates, diffs, and filtering to visible elements only. The listing is incomplete, as indicated by an ellipsis. It supports text-observation scope and the presence of history in the agent configuration, not necessarily the retriever.

### Figure 17 — Defense retrieval prompt, p. 24

The prompt warns about information theft, asks for task-relevant lines, and asks for malicious content removal. It also mentions screenshots even though F16 disables screenshot use. The evaluated modality is therefore taken from the experiment description and configuration, not inferred from that unused prompt wording. The listing is evidence about the defense, not an instruction to this analysis.

### Figure 18 — Banner attack in AxTree, p. 25

## 12. Diagram / architecture interpretation

F1 and F2 show complementary levels of the same system. F1 establishes the two model roles; F2 shows the actual transformation from page text to selected text. The task goal influences which lines are retained. Numbering is an indexing operation, not a semantic rewrite of the page. The retriever selects ranges, and post-processing extracts original content within them. The larger model then decides an action. A newly observed state begins another iteration.

The architecture's principal data boundary is between the original observation and the pruned observation. The authors intend to remove irrelevant and attack-bearing material before the action model sees it. However, the browser itself retains its actual state: filtering the textual observation does not close a popup, remove a DOM element, or restore background interaction. That distinction explains the popup result. The representation can omit a threat while the environment continues to obstruct execution. [A/D; pp. 7–8]

Line-level removal also creates a granularity problem. If a legitimate control and malicious instructions occupy the same textual element, selecting that element retains both, whereas deleting it may remove the only way to proceed. F22 is the concrete example. Future cleaning of text within the element is proposed, but the evaluated method primarily selects lines rather than demonstrating such element-level repair.

## 13. Equations and mathematical concepts

### Observation pruning, p. 5

The unnumbered formula is **Pruning(o_i)=1−|o_r|/|o_i|**. Here o_i is the original observation, o_r is the retrieved observation, and vertical bars indicate token count. The input is two observation lengths; the output is the removed fraction, which is multiplied by 100 when expressed as a percentage. Equal lengths give zero pruning; smaller retrieved lengths give positive pruning. The original length must be nonzero for the division to be defined. The paper does not discuss empty-observation handling.

### Simplified cost model, pp. 16–17

The agent policy is denoted π with parameters θ_L; the retriever policy has parameters θ_S, with θ_S much smaller than θ_L. Parameter counts are not reported. C_L and C_S are the respective model input costs per token, or equivalently consistently scaled costs per million tokens. FocusAgent processes the original observation with the small model and the retained observation with the large model:

**Cost_Focus=C_S|o_i|+C_L|o_r|.**

The baseline cost is **Cost_Base=C_L|o_i|**. Requiring FocusAgent not to cost more gives **C_S|o_i|+C_L|o_r|≤C_L|o_i|**. Substituting retained length |o_r|=α|o_i| and dividing by nonzero |o_i| yields **C_S+C_Lα≤C_L**, hence Eq. (1): **α≤(C_L−C_S)/C_L**.

With C_S=0.4 and C_L=2 USD per million tokens, α≤0.8. Thus at least 20% of original tokens must be removed for non-increasing observation-input cost under these assumptions. At exactly 20%, the equation gives break-even, not strict savings. Strict savings require more than 20% removal.

There is a notation inconsistency: Appendix F calls α a pruning ratio, but the substitution and final 1−α expression make it a **retained fraction**, whereas the metric on p. 5 uses pruning to mean removed fraction. The mathematics is understandable when α is read as retained fraction, but the terminology should not be silently harmonized.

The initial inequality |o_r|≤α|o_i| is subsequently used as an equality. Reading α as the actual retained fraction reproduces the derivation; if it is merely an upper bound, the resulting condition is sufficient for the modeled comparison. This distinction is analyst interpretation [D].

The equation excludes API latency, full prompt processing, and any explicitly modeled output-generation charge. It also does not guarantee equivalent numbers of actions across agents. Aggregate experiment costs and per-step costs therefore need separate interpretation. No mathematical security guarantee is provided.

## 14. Interpretation and discussion

The strongest supported finding is that selective LLM retrieval can remove substantial page text while retaining much more observed task success than the tested embedding and keyword baselines. The main benchmark data support a trade-off: lower modeled input cost in exchange for modest to several-point SR reductions, depending on backbone and benchmark. They do not establish exact performance equivalence.

Security has two dimensions in the results. One is avoiding the attacker's requested behavior; the other is maintaining the user's ability to finish the task. Banner removal addresses both reasonably well for GPT-4.1 in the reported setting. Popup removal mainly addresses the first. The overlay remains, and the close control itself contains injection text. The guard establishes an even more extreme version of the same distinction: no successful attacks but no successful tasks under attack.

For the user's research question, **analyst inference [D]** is that web agents face an additional environmental instruction channel and must turn their reading into actions. The printed attacks show page metadata impersonating authoritative instructions and trying to cause navigation away from the user's task. Dynamic browser state also creates operational disruption even when the model rejects or does not see the malicious instruction. This paper supplies mechanism-level relevance, not direct empirical evidence that the same backbone is more vulnerable as an agent than as a standalone conversational model.

## 15. Contributions and novelty

**Conceptual:** treat observation relevance as dependent on the current task and page state, rather than only lexical or embedding similarity. **Methodological/algorithmic:** number AxTree lines, use a lightweight LLM to select ranges, and reconstruct a reduced observation. **Systems:** insert a retrieval stage before an existing action-prediction agent. **Security:** augment that stage with attack warnings and malicious-content removal rather than stopping every detected attack. **Empirical:** compare backbones, retrieval approaches, prompting policies, formatting policies, security conditions, and distributional behavior.

The authors call the approach simple and novel, and state three contributions on p. 2. This analysis can report that positioning but cannot independently verify priority against the outside literature. No new dataset, theorem, training algorithm, or comprehensive security proof is supplied. Printed prompts and configuration aid implementation understanding but are not a complete executable implementation.

## 16. Limitations

### Authors' stated limitations

Appendix A explicitly identifies dependence on prompt engineering and evolving LLM behavior; inability to ensure a fully clean webpage with no residual malicious content; and lack of testing beyond 128k retriever context. [A; p. 12]

The security discussion also acknowledges residual successful banner attacks, especially attack-dominated 404 and image-only pages; popup-induced blocking despite low ASR; and an ASR/TSR trade-off they did not eliminate. The cost appendix explicitly excludes API latency and full-prompt processing from its simplified estimate. [A; pp. 8, 16]

### Additional evidence-based analyst observations

[D] The paper does not directly compare standalone LLMs and agents. Security evidence covers 114 Reddit tasks and two separate text-only attack types, so it cannot support unrestricted conclusions about agent security. The retriever itself sees untrusted content. Warning-only Claude performs better than retrieval on popup utility in T3. No attack-free equivalence test, detailed per-cell security uncertainty, adaptive attack evaluation, or complete success predicate is supplied.

[D] The classic retrieval comparison changes selection mechanism and output-length policy: fixed top-10 chunks contrast with dynamic LLM-selected spans. Differences cannot be assigned exclusively to reasoning capability. Main benchmark and security Reddit subsets differ. Repeated numerical and caption inconsistencies limit precise reproduction. Raw observations, detailed run logs, complete agent prompts, software versions, and exact decoding parameters are not available in the supplied material.

## 17. Threats to validity

The following labels are analyst organization [D], not terms attributed to the authors.

**Internal validity:** the results compare bundled configurations. LLM retrieval, dynamic length selection, preservation of tree continuity, and differing history policies can all influence outcomes. The embedding/BM25 explanation is plausible but not experimentally isolated. Popup task failures are supported by the reported mechanism and printed example, but no exhaustive failure count by mechanism is supplied.

**Construct validity:** ASR captures attack success, not every harmful consequence. TSR captures legitimate completion, not comprehensive safety. A low ASR can coexist with practical loss of service, as the popup rows demonstrate. Modeled input-token cost is not total deployed operating cost or elapsed time.

**Statistical conclusion validity:** SE is supplied for main SR and a range for security results, but no significance tests, confidence intervals, equivalence margins, or task-cluster dependence treatment are specified. Ten seeds per WorkArena task are repeated instances of tasks, not 330 necessarily independent task types. Small differences should remain observed differences rather than proven improvements.

**External/ecological validity:** benchmarks, selected tasks, text observations, step budgets, and fixed backbones constrain generalization. Screenshot examples do not establish multimodal defense effectiveness. Untested over-128k processing and absent combined/adaptive attack evaluation are material boundaries.

**Reproducibility:** prompts, settings, counts, chunk sizes, limits, and prices help reconstruction. Missing model snapshots, framework versions, exact seeds, run artifacts, and inconsistent numbers prevent full reproduction from this paper alone. No reproduction was performed here.

## 18. Future work and open questions

### A. Explicit author proposals

The authors propose further improving the unresolved security/utility trade-off and cleaning malicious content from the element carrying it before sending the element to the agent, particularly the contaminated popup close button. They describe sequential processing of over-context AxTree parts and combining ranges, while admitting that this longer-context setup was not tested. They suggest that more capable small models may better handle pruning and that more sophisticated attacks are necessary for robust evaluation. [A; pp. 4, 8, 12]

### B. Additional analyst open questions

[D] Can a defense preserve a control's identifier and legitimate function while removing its malicious label? How robust is the retriever against attacks targeted directly at line selection? Can it recover useful context on error pages dominated by malicious text? Does the advantage persist when classic retrieval is allowed dynamic output lengths and matched structural formatting? What happens under combined or adaptive attacks? How do output-token costs, latency, and changing action counts alter savings? How would a controlled same-backbone standalone-versus-agent evaluation separate environmental exposure from action capability? None of these questions is answered by the supplied experiments.

## 22. Very simple explanation — Explain Like I'm 15

Imagine an assistant trying to use a website for you. Before every click, it receives a very long description of everything on the page. Most of that description may be unrelated to your request. Worse, someone can hide text in the page that tells the assistant to abandon your job and follow a fake instruction.

FocusAgent adds a smaller assistant whose job is to choose which lines the main assistant should read. Keeping useful controls and removing unrelated text can make the main assistant's input cheaper. In the reported tests, it removes about half or more of the page-description tokens, with somewhat lower task success than the full-context agent.

For security, the smaller assistant also tries to remove attack instructions. This works well against the tested banners. Popups expose the harder problem: the assistant may avoid the attack but still fail your task because the popup blocks the page. The button needed to close it can itself carry malicious text. Hiding the popup from the assistant's description does not make the real popup disappear.

This helps explain why acting on websites creates additional security problems: the assistant reads material controlled by other people and must use it to decide real actions. However, this paper does not test whether the same language model is more vulnerable as a web agent than as an ordinary chatbot. It demonstrates a relevant mechanism and a partial defense, not that direct comparison.

claims.statement: FocusAgent applies a lightweight LLM retriever to each step's observation, selects numbered line ranges, and passes the reduced observation to the action-predicting agent.
The chosen retrieval strategy uses soft prompting with the task goal and current observation, omitting interaction history from the retriever.
Table 1 reports GPT-4.1 WorkArena success of 53.0% for GenericAgent-BT and 51.5% for FocusAgent, with FocusAgent pruning 51% and modeled cost falling from $55.6 to $45.1 across 330 task instances.

On WorkArena with GPT-4.1 backbone, the tested embedding retriever achieves 40.3% success versus 51.5% for FocusAgent; the authors hypothesize that classic similarity retrieval misses state-relevant content.
The security evaluation studies separate text-only banner and popup attacks, rather than combined attacks or a general multimodal attack suite.

In Table 3's 114-task Reddit evaluation, GPT-4.1 banner ASR/TSR changes from 32.4%/34.8% for GenericAgent to 0.9%/42.1% for DefenseFocusAgent; these results concern the warning-augmented retrieval variant.
Low popup attack success does not preserve practical task completion: DefenseFocusAgent reports GPT-4.1 ASR 1.0% and TSR 2.0%, and the authors explain that the popup blocks background actions.

Retrieval is not uniformly the best popup defense in Table 3: warning-only Claude DefenseGenericAgent has ASR 0% and TSR 20.2%, compared with retrieval-based Claude DefenseFocusAgent at ASR 0.9% and TSR 1.8%.

The prompt ablation favors explicit conservative uncertainty handling: soft prompting has the highest observed success, while more aggressive pruning reduces observed task performance, particularly on the Reddit subset.
The authors acknowledge that removing attack content does not ensure a completely clean webpage without residual malicious content.
Processing retriever contexts longer than 128k tokens is not experimentally validated in the supplied work, although the authors describe a sequential splitting extension.

The simplified observation-input cost model reaches break-even at at least 20% removal when the small-model price is $0.40 and the large-model price is $2 per million tokens; the estimate excludes API latency and full-prompt processing.
Table 5's displayed GPT-5-mini retrieval costs imply a 31.47% total-cost reduction: 100×(55.6−38.1)/55.6, which disagrees with the table's −46% label.

For the user’s agent-versus-standalone research question, the paper supports a mechanism-level inference: web agents encounter indirect malicious instructions in their operational environment and can convert that content into actions. It does not directly measure relative vulnerability against standalone LLMs.

Figure 22 supports a control-content entanglement mechanism: the popup close button is clickable, but its textual label carries malicious instructions, so retaining the necessary control can also expose the action model to attack-bearing content.
